extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism (readers of Aristotle's Poetics / poetics theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and applying Aristotle's theoretical criteria for poetry and drama (esp. tragedy, epic, comedy) — including principles of imitation, diction, metre, structure, and the constituent parts of tragedy. Useful for literary analysis or creative-writing grounded in classical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Language (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction, or Language in general. An analysis of the parts of speech, and other grammatical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on choice of words and grammatical construction as a distinct aspect of poetic/artistic craft; includes attention to parts of speech and fine grammatical detail when evaluating language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic Diction. The words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry : including Metaphor, in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether vocabulary and modes of speech suit the demands of poetry; judge admissibility of metaphors and other figures. (The edition notes an interpolated passage on Gender of Nouns.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of language with perspicuity
rubrics_metrics.description: How Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic language should be elevated where appropriate but maintain clarity; balance grandeur with intelligibility so meaning is not obscured by ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Tragedy & Epic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry and Tragedy agree in Unity of Action: this unity distinguishes them from History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plot coherence by whether the work presents a single, unified action rather than a disconnected series of events; historical breadth vs poetic unity is a criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy — key differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of difference enumerated: (1) the length of the poem; (2) the metre; (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing or composing epic and tragic forms, assess: appropriate scope/length (epic larger), correct metre (epic hexameter vs tragedy's metres), and the poet's skill at making improbable events seem plausible (verisimilitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Response to Critical Objections / Poetic Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical Objections brought against Poetry, and the principles on which they are to be answered. In particular, an elucidation of the meaning of Poetic Truth, and its difference from common reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetic work with an understanding that 'poetic truth' differs from literal factual truth; objections based on literalness should be answered using principles distinguishing poetic plausibility and expressive truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative worth of Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A general estimate of the comparative worth of Epic Poetry and Tragedy. The alleged defects of Tragedy are not essential to it. Its positive merits entitle it to the higher rank of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing literary value, consider Tragedy's merits (as articulated) relative to Epic's; alleged defects may be non-essential and should not alone determine rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three distinguishing differences of imitation arts
rubrics_metrics.description: They differ, however, from one another in three respects,—the medium, the objects, the manner or mode of imitation, being in each case distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three axes (medium, objects, manner) as primary classificatory/evaluative dimensions when analyzing or composing different poetic/performative arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the arts above mentioned, taken as a whole, the imitation is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony,' either singly or combined. (E.g., music uses 'harmony' and rhythm alone; dancing uses rhythm alone; language imitates by prose or verse.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which medium(s) the piece employs and whether those media are effectively used; judge appropriateness of combining (or isolating) rhythm, language, and harmony for the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (types of men in action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the objects of imitation are men in action, and these men must be either of a higher or a lower type (goodness and badness being distinguishing marks), we must represent men either as better than in real life, or as worse, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characterization by its type: does the work portray characters elevated, degraded, or true-to-life? Examples: Homer makes men better, Cleophon as they are, Hegemon worse. The ethical/moral type chosen is a deliberate aesthetic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration—in which case he can either take another personality as Homer does, or speak in his own person—or he may present all his characters as living and moving before us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging voice and presentation, assess whether narration or enactment better serves the work's aims and whether the chosen manner is executed convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's psychological origins (imitation & harmony instinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry in general seems to have sprung from two causes... First, the instinct of imitation is implanted in man from childhood... Next, there is the instinct for 'harmony' and rhythm, metres being manifestly sections of rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the natural human pleasures (learning via imitation; pleasure in rhythm/harmony) as foundations for assessing why a poetic element succeeds or fails with audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy (formal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this formal definition to evaluate tragic works: seriousness, completeness, magnitude of action; use of ornament (rhythm/harmony/song) across parts; enactment over narration; and emotional effect (pity/fear leading to catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent parts of Tragedy (spectacle, song, diction, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: As tragic imitation implies persons acting, it necessarily follows, in the first place, that Spectacular equipment will be a part of Tragedy. Next, Song and Diction, for these are the medium of imitation. By 'Diction' ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the play's spectacle (stagecraft), the songs/choral elements, and diction (language choices) as distinct but integrated components; consider which parts are rendered in verse vs song and how they function together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (Tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy endeavours, as far as possible, to confine itself to a single revolution of the sun, or but slightly to exceed this limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess temporal unity: whether the dramatic action stays within a compact time-frame to preserve unity and intensity, or if temporal expansion weakens dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's development/history (actors, chorus, scenic art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy advanced by slow degrees; Aeschylus introduced a second actor; he diminished the importance of the Chorus, and assigned the leading part to the dialogue. Sophocles raised the number of actors to three, and added scene-painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing forms or historic practices, consider how changes in actor number, chorus function, and scenic presentation affect dramatic focus and the balance between dialogue and choral/spectacular elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter appropriateness (iambic vs hexameter etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The iambic is, of all measures, the most colloquial: we see it in the fact that conversational speech runs into iambic lines more frequently than into any other kind of verse; rarely into hexameters... Epic admits but one kind of metre (hexameter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether meter fits voice and function: use iambic for colloquial/dialogue-like elements; hexameter for epic narrative; assess whether metre supports the intended register and mode of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic imitation and the Ludicrous
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type — not, however, in the full sense of the word bad, the Ludicrous being merely a subdivision of the ugly. It consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comedic effect by whether the ludicrous (non-painful ugliness/defect) is properly presented; judge whether character depiction aims intentionally at degradation, satire, or general lampoon and whether it achieves laughter without cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic characteristics (narrative form, unlimited time, single metre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry admits but one kind of metre, and is narrative in form... Epic action has no limits of time. Of their constituent parts some are common to both, some peculiar to Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess epic works for narrative scope, consistent use of metre (traditionally hexameter), and capacity to encompass wider temporal/spatial dimensions compared to drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of poetic means in certain forms
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some arts which employ all the means above mentioned,—namely, rhythm, tune, and metre. Such are Dithyrambic and Nomic poetry, and also Tragedy and Comedy; but between them the difference is, that in the first two cases these means are all employed in combination, in the latter, now one means is employed, now another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating works like dithyrambs, nomes, tragedy, or comedy, note whether rhythm, tune, and metre are combined or selectively used and whether that combination is coherent and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming/genre vs metre (practical caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: People ... speak of elegiac poets, or epic (that is, hexameter) poets, as if it were not the imitation that makes the poet, but the verse that entitles them all indiscriminately to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about genre labels based solely on metre — evaluate a creator by the mode of imitation and subject, not merely by the verse-form employed.
